newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Fujimori in Bolivia, hostage mediator visits jail.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori in Bolivia, hostage mediator visits jail.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori met for talks late on Friday with his Bolivian counterpart on the deadlocked Lima hostage crisis, while a key mediator visited the guerrilla hostage-takers' leader in jail.

Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, member of a three-man mediation team in the 109-day standoff, visited a naval base in the port of Callao where Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Victor Polay and other MRTA leaders are held.
Cipriani spoke to Polay in the prison during the Friday evening visit, local radio said, though Cipriani had no comment.
The visit to the prison led to speculation that Cipriani, facing a deadlock in talks with the MRTA to free the 72 hostages, was taking negotiations directly to the MRTA leadership.
About 20 MRTA guerrillas stormed a cocktail party at the Japanese ambassador's residence on Dec. 17 and took the guests hostage to demand freedom for about 450 jailed comrades.
They are still holding a 72 Cabinet ministers, ambassadors, military brass and Japanese businessmen.

Fujimori, grappling with the greatest challenge to his authority since taking office in 1990, arrived in the Bolivian city of Santa Cruz for talks with President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada on the standoff.

Signalling flexibility, a top Bolivian official said his government might consider easing prison terms for Peruvian Marxist rebels held in jails as a way to help win the release of the lone Bolivian hostage, ambassador Jorge Gumucio.
"We don't have an official petition in that regard from the MRTA, but if that were the case, the government would consider it," Information Minister Mauricio Antezana told reporters.

But Bolivian President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada said his government could not bow to MRTA demands for outright freedom for the four MRTA rebels jailed in Bolivia, echoing Fujimori's own stand on the 450 MRTA prisoners in Peruvian jails.
"We are barred by law from freeing people who are subject to the judiciary," Sanchez de Lozada said after Fujimori arrived in the humid city in the Amazon lowlands.

"The only request I will make is that everything that is humanly possible be made in order to find a peaceful solution, although I expect him (Fujimori) to keep telling me to be patient and keep up the spirit," he told reporters.

Fujimori had no comment for journalists before going straight into talks and later dinner with Sanchez de Lozada. The two leaders will also discuss plans for an Andean summit in Sucre, Bolivia, in late April and visit the drug-producing Chapare area on Saturday, Antezana said.
At the besieged residence in Lima's wealthy San Isidro district, police continued to bear down on curious onlookers and reporters who strayed too close to the house.
A Peruvian photographer for Agence France-Presse, Cristobal Bouroncle, was briefly detained by police near the residence allegedly for not carrying the proper credentials.
This week several people, including three Austrians and an American, were arrested for taking pictures in the area without official press credentials, police said. All were later released.

A secret intelligence report obtained by Reuters said new information suggested Congress President Victor Joy Way, two legislators and five mayors -- all harsh critics of the MRTA -- might be targeted for attacks by rebel commandos.
Joy Way was expected to fly to Tokyo this month for hostage crisis talks with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
